5-6: A division with a remainder: the number that was divided.
Pages in a range whose numbers divide by a given number.
A loop of stations: where a train is after a given number of stops.
Seats numbered row by row: the row and the place of a given seat.
The smallest number that leaves the same remainder for several divisors.
The rule of 3 or 9: which digit makes a number divide, or the remainder of a long number of repeated digits.
Sharing as equally as possible: the most that can be left over.
Scores of two kinds, such as 3 and 8 points: the largest total that cannot be made.
The last digit of a power, from the cycle of last digits.
The number of divisors of a number.
A bill whose items all come in multiples of 3, such as one thing at 3 and six of another: a total that is not a multiple of 3 cannot be right.
Different whole numbers whose sum divides by each of them, such as 1, 2 and 3: each new number can be the sum of all before it.
Statements that a number divides by several numbers, all true but one: a statement that would make all the others true must be the false one.
A number told by the sum of its few smallest divisors, or of its two largest: 1 comes first, then its smallest prime, and the largest is the number itself.
Lockers opened and closed by everyone whose number divides theirs: those left open have an odd number of divisors, which only squares have.
Different digits split into two groups with equal products: a prime such as 5 or 7 found in one digit only would have to be on both sides, so it cannot be done.
Steps of two lengths with no common divisor but 1, such as 37 left and 47 right: the fewest moves ending one unit to a given side of the start, the side changing the answer.
A power of ten as a product of two numbers with no zero digit: all its twos go into one and all its fives into the other, so it works only if neither of those powers has a 0.
A long product of whole numbers: how many times it divides by 2, or how many zeros it ends with, from the twos and fives its factors hold.
Two numbers with a given sum and no common divisor but 1: the largest product comes from the closest such pair.
